result: Prior to this study, the space-time wiring model for direction selectivity in starburst amacrine cells was proposed but lacked direct experimental verification of kinetically distinct glutamate inputs along dendrites.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C23, and C31 consistently establish the state of the field prior to this work. These claims accurately represent the gap in knowledge that motivated the study, supported by appropriate citations to prior literature.

result: Direct iGluSnFR imaging revealed that glutamate signals measured from proximal starburst dendrites were significantly more sustained compared to distal dendrites, with the sustained/transient index (STi) decreasing systematically with distance from the soma.
evaluation: Claims C3, C35, C36, and C39 present quantitative experimental data with appropriate statistical tests (p<0.001, t-test) showing clear kinetic differences between proximal and distal inputs. The measurements are supported by Figures 1 and 2, with adequate sample sizes (n=20 dendrites, 242 proximal ROIs, 563 distal ROIs). C122 correctly identifies this as the first direct evidence for the space-time wiring model.

result: Kinetic differences between proximal and distal inputs were observed across a range of stimulus sizes (100-800 μm), with differences most pronounced for stimuli >200 μm in diameter.
evaluation: Claims C4, C57, and C93 are supported by systematic experimental data across multiple stimulus sizes shown in Figure 4. Statistical analysis (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, p<0.001) confirms significant differences. The observation that smallest stimuli (~50 μm) did not show differences reconciles apparent contradictions with prior work (C91-C93).

result: Kinetic differences between proximal and distal inputs persisted in the presence of pharmacological blockade of inhibitory pathways, indicating that excitatory rather than inhibitory network mechanisms primarily shape these differences.
evaluation: Claims C5, C59, and C60 are supported by pharmacological experiments using GABA and glutamate receptor antagonists (Figure 4). The persistence of kinetic differences under blockade (p<0.001, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test) provides strong evidence that inhibition is not required for generating these differences, though C96-C97 appropriately note this was unexpected given prior literature.

result: Under inhibitory receptor blockade, iGluSnFR responses showed unexpected lateral excitation extending beyond BC dendritic field sizes, likely attributable to electrical coupling between bipolar cells and amacrine cells.
evaluation: Claims C61-C64 describe experimental observations from pharmacological experiments with appropriate statistical support (p<0.01). C65 and C99 provide reasonable mechanistic interpretations supported by citations to prior work on electrical coupling. However, C103 acknowledges that differential coupling between BC7 and BC5 remains untested, appropriately limiting the strength of this conclusion.

result: Direct imaging of BC7 terminals confirmed sustained glutamate release kinetics, consistent with anatomical evidence that BC7s provide proximal input to starburst dendrites.
evaluation: Claims C43-C44 establish anatomical connectivity from prior work. C46-C48 provide direct experimental evidence from BC7 imaging (Figure 3) showing sustained responses. C49 appropriately concludes BC7s are the source of sustained proximal input. However, C50 acknowledges a limitation: inability to image BC5s prevents direct confirmation they provide transient distal input.

result: White-noise stimulation revealed biphasic impulse responses for both proximal and distal inputs, suggesting that under high-frequency continuous stimulation, input kinetics are unlikely to contribute to direction selectivity.
evaluation: Claims C51-C52 present experimental observations from white-noise experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 2). C53 provides a reasonable mechanistic interpretation. C55 draws an appropriate conclusion about the stimulus-dependence of the kinetic mechanism, though this somewhat limits the generality of the main findings.

result: Temporal deconvolution analysis estimated that steady-state vesicle release rates were approximately 3 times higher at proximal sites (~3 vesicles/s) compared to distal sites (~1 vesicle/s), with peak rates of 5-10 vesicles/s.
evaluation: Claims C67-C68 describe the deconvolution method and validation. C69-C70 and C6 present the key quantitative findings. However, C106 acknowledges critical assumptions (linear superposition, no glutamate buildup) that may not hold. The estimates in C107-C108 are compared to prior work for plausibility, but the method's validity depends on untested assumptions about iGluSnFR properties (C104). Additional validation would strengthen these quantitative claims.

result: A biophysically-constrained computational model demonstrated that experimentally-determined input kinetics contribute to direction selectivity primarily at low stimulus velocities (<0.5 mm/s).
evaluation: Claims C71-C72 justify the modeling approach based on prior work. C73-C74 show the model recapitulates experimental observations. C75-C76 and C7 present the key finding about velocity dependence. C85 and C115 appropriately conclude the space-time wiring model has merit under specific conditions. The model is well-constrained by experimental data, though C112 notes intrinsic starburst properties remain poorly defined.

result: Computational modeling showed that swapping the kinetics of proximal and distal inputs reversed directional preference, and that direction selectivity decreased when all inputs were made uniform or when sustained inputs were incrementally converted to transient.
evaluation: Claims C77-C82 present systematic computational manipulations with appropriate statistical analysis (ANOVA p<0.05, t-test p<0.0005). C84 shows linear relationships between spatial offset and DSi (R²≈0.21-0.27). These modeling results provide strong support for the importance of kinetic diversity, though the modest R² values suggest other factors also contribute.

result: The combined experimental and modeling results provide direct support for the space-time wiring model for direction selectivity in starburst amacrine cells.
evaluation: Claims C8, C90, and C122 represent the main conclusion of the study. This is well-supported by the convergent experimental evidence (C3-C5, C46-C49) and computational modeling (C7, C77-C82). However, the conclusion is appropriately qualified by C55, C76, C85, and C115, which limit the model's applicability to specific stimulus conditions (large, slow-moving objects).

result: Experimentally observed direction selectivity in starbursts occurs across a wide range of velocities (100-2000 μm/s), indicating that additional mechanisms beyond input kinetics are involved.
evaluation: Claims C113-C114 appropriately acknowledge limitations of the kinetic mechanism based on comparison to prior experimental observations. This is an important caveat that prevents overinterpretation of the modeling results, which show kinetic contributions primarily at low velocities.

result: The sustained/transient index was independent of response amplitude, and latencies and rise times were similar for proximal and distal sites, indicating that kinetic differences are not due to signal-to-noise issues or transmission delays.
evaluation: Claims C40-C42 address important controls. C40 is supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1 showing no correlation between STi and amplitude. C41-C42 are supported by Figure 2D-E. These controls strengthen confidence that the observed kinetic differences reflect genuine biological properties rather than technical artifacts.

result: The apparent contradiction with prior studies showing similar BC kinetics is explained by differences in stimulus parameters, specifically that kinetic differences emerge for larger stimuli but not for small spots covering only the BC receptive field.
evaluation: Claims C91-C94 appropriately reconcile the current findings with prior work (Franke et al., 2017). The explanation is supported by the systematic stimulus size experiments (C57, C93) and citations to prior work showing stimulus-dependent kinetic diversity (C94). This demonstrates careful consideration of the literature.

result: Kinetic differences persist when rod-mediated signals are blocked by CNQX, indicating they cannot be attributed solely to rod/cone vision differences.
evaluation: Claim C98 presents an important control experiment ruling out an alternative explanation. The result is supported by citation to prior work (Awatramani and Slaughter, 2000) showing similar findings. This strengthens the conclusion that kinetic differences reflect intrinsic properties of BC types rather than photoreceptor input differences.

result: Electrical coupling between bipolar cells and between BCs and amacrine cells may contribute to kinetic differences, though whether BC7 and BC5 have different coupling patterns remains untested.
evaluation: Claims C100-C102 cite prior work on electrical coupling and its effects. However, C103 explicitly acknowledges that differential coupling between BC7 and BC5 remains untested. This is presented as a plausible mechanism but lacks direct experimental support in this study. The speculation is reasonable but requires future validation.

result: Despite potential complexities in interpreting iGluSnFR signals, prior studies have shown these signals reflect local glutamate release from individual BC terminals.
evaluation: Claim C104 appropriately acknowledges complexities in interpreting iGluSnFR signals. C105 cites multiple prior studies validating that iGluSnFR signals reflect local release despite uniform expression. This provides important context for interpreting the experimental results, though some uncertainty remains about quantitative accuracy.

result: The modeling approach differs from prior optimization-based and phenomenological models by using experimentally-constrained parameters, though starburst intrinsic properties remain poorly defined.
evaluation: Claims C110-C111 appropriately distinguish this modeling approach from prior work through citations. C112 acknowledges an important limitation: intrinsic starburst properties are poorly defined. This is an honest assessment of model limitations that appropriately qualifies the conclusions.

result: For other stimulus types such as radial motion or suddenly emerging stimuli, inhibitory surrounds of BCs may enhance motion sensitivity in more complex ways.
evaluation: Claim C116 is speculative, supported only by citations to recent work (Gaynes et al., 2022; Strauss et al., 2022). This represents a reasonable hypothesis about stimulus-dependent mechanisms but is not directly tested in this study. It appropriately qualifies the scope of the current findings.
